## Purpose

Placeholder. This section will state why the work was done, the key takeaway, and who it is for.

The argument to make here: binder design campaigns run with ESMFold2 return mostly α-helical binders, and a designer who needs a different fold has no obvious knob to turn. We add a secondary-structure term to the design loss, show what it buys and what it costs, and report whether the resulting designs are worth trialing.

Primary audience: people running structure-prediction-based binder design campaigns, and people interested in what can be steered in a folding model after training.

Placeholder. Three claims to establish, each needing citations added to `ref.bib`:

1. **Binder design tends to be α-rich.** Design pipelines built on structure predictors return helical binders far more often than any other fold class. To write: how general this is across pipelines, and what is already known about why.

## ESMFold2 designs are biased towards α-helix

The ESMFold2 preprint demonstrates binder design on five targets: the EGFR domain III, the PDGFRβ D2–D3 tandem, the PD-L1 and CTLA-4 IgV domains, and the CD45 d3–d4 tandem. Those are the five used here. Running the algorithm unmodified against each, 30 designs per target at 150 optimization steps, gives 150 binders whose secondary structure can be measured directly from the predicted complex.

For a comparison set we queried the RCSB for experimentally determined heterodimers and kept the chains of 60–200 residues, the range the design loop samples binder lengths from. That gives 2,098 natural binder chains, each solved in complex with its partner. Short proteins are helix-biased on their own, so the natural set is resampled to match the length distribution of the designs rather than pooled across lengths.

@fig-composition sets the two side by side across the length range, in each of the three states.

The median design is **80% helix**, against **31%** for a length-matched natural binder; Cliff's delta is **+0.60**, above the conventional threshold for a large effect. The excess holds in every length bin of @fig-composition-1, so it is not an artifact of the designs and the natural set occupying different parts of the length range.

Sheet runs the other way. The deficit holds in every bin of @fig-composition-2, though the design bars carry visibly wider standard errors than the natural ones: the designs that do form sheet form a lot of it, so a bin mean rests on a handful of high values against many zeros.

Loop shows the largest separation of the three, at Cliff's delta −0.81: designs average 21% loop against 40% for natural binders, and @fig-composition-3 shows the gap in every bin. So the helix is displacing irregular structure as much as it is displacing sheet. This is also the panel most exposed to the confound described below, because predicted structures tend to have cleaner secondary structure than experimental ones, which would suppress loop specifically. It should be read as consistent with the helix result rather than as independent evidence for it.

The pattern holds on every target. Median helix ranges from 0.75 to 0.84 across the five, and median sheet is zero on all five, including the four whose own fold is entirely β. The preference is therefore a property of the design procedure rather than a response to the target. Mean helix, 0.67, sits below the median, so a minority of designs are considerably less helical than the rest: this is a central tendency, not a floor.

:::{.callout-note collapse="true" title="How secondary structure is assigned, and what to distrust about the comparison"}
Labels come from [`pydssp`](https://github.com/ShintaroMinami/PyDSSP), a Kabsch–Sander implementation, collapsed to three states and reported as a fraction of binder residues. Both sides go through the same `analysis.secondary_structure` code, so the two are not measured by two different implementations of DSSP. Only residues with a complete N, Cα, C and O backbone are labelled, so a residue missing from a model is missing from its denominator too.

The reference set comes from one RCSB query, recorded in `data/reference/natural_binder_search_hits.json` and rerunnable with `analysis.rcsb.build`: X-ray entries at 2.5 Å or better, exactly two polymer entities, heteromeric, a named source organism that is not "synthetic construct", and at least one entity of 60–200 residues, which is the range the design loop samples binder lengths from. Entities are clustered at 30% sequence identity and one representative per cluster is kept. That leaves 2,098 chains from 1,813 entries at median resolution 2.00 Å. Where both chains of an entry are in range, 53% of them, each takes its turn as the binder.

Now the things worth distrusting.

**"Binder" is a label we impose.** In a natural heterodimer neither chain is the binder; both are partners. Calling the 60–200-residue chain the binder is an analogy to the design setting, not a fact about the complex.

**Some partners are peptides, not domains.** Target chains run from 8 to 1,020 residues, and 15% are short enough to flag as peptide targets. A 100-residue protein gripping an 8-residue peptide is a different structural problem from a designed minibinder against a folded domain. These are flagged in the table rather than removed, so the flag can be used to test sensitivity.

**Some interfaces may not be real.** 13% are small enough to be crystal packing rather than function. Also flagged rather than removed.

**"Natural" is approximate.** 1% of binders and 3% of targets read as engineered scaffolds by description. Excluding "synthetic construct" as a source organism catches the obvious cases, not the subtle ones.

**The PDB is a convenience sample.** X-ray at 2.5 Å or better favours proteins that crystallise well, which favours compact, rigid, often β-rich folds, and excludes cryo-EM and NMR entirely. 31% of binders are human. This is a sample of the binders that got solved, not of binders.

**Clustering at 30% identity does not remove structural redundancy.** Immunoglobulin-like folds recur across clusters that share little sequence.

**Composition is measured over resolved residues only**, a median 96% of each construct, which biases the natural coil fraction downward and makes the natural set look more ordered than the protein is in solution.

**The two sides sit on different kinds of coordinates.** The natural set is experimental; the designs are ESMFold2's own prediction, and predicted structures tend to have idealised secondary structure. That would inflate both helix *and* sheet in the designs, so it cannot explain a sheet deficit, but it does mean the coil comparison should be read loosely.
:::

## A loss term steers designs out of the α-rich basin

The intervention tested here is a term added to the objective a design run minimizes, so the loop and the objective it already carries come first.


### How ESMFold2 designs a binder

Nothing about the model changes. Design is inference-time optimization: the weights of every network involved stay frozen, and the only thing that moves is the binder's own sequence. A run starts from the target sequence and a binder length drawn uniformly from 60 to 200 residues, and holds the binder's identity as a tensor of per-position amino-acid logits. The target is a fixed one-hot encoding that no gradient reaches.

Each of the 150 steps softmaxes those logits into a soft sequence, folds the target and the soft binder together with ESMFold2, and reads the predicted Cα–Cα distogram — a distribution over 128 distance bins for every residue pair. The objective is computed from that distogram, and its gradient is taken back through the folding stack to the logits. So the search is a structure-prediction model being run backwards: the thing being asked for is a sequence whose predicted structure scores well.

A sequence that satisfies a geometric objective need not look like a protein, so a second gradient comes from ESMC, scoring the binder's pseudo-perplexity under a masked-language model over four sampled mask passes. ESMC is the sequence prior rather than the search: it constrains what the structural objective is allowed to ask for. The two gradients are separately normalized to unit norm per position and summed in a 1 to 0.15 ratio, then applied by SGD. ESMC also sits inside ESMFold2 as its language-model trunk, and the two share those weights in memory.

The softmax temperature follows a cosine schedule from 1 down to 0.01, so early steps optimize a genuinely mixed sequence and late steps a nearly discrete one. Each step draws one of two ESMFold2 replicates at random.

When the run ends, the best sequence is refolded by four ESMFold2 critic models at higher sampling, and those critics supply every interface pTM and per-chain pLDDT quoted below. The critique is therefore an estimate from the same architecture that ran the search, at a different sampling budget, which bounds what any confidence number below can settle on its own.

Across every arm in this section the target, the seed, the binder length, the step count, the learning rate, the temperature schedule and the critics are identical. The only thing that differs is the objective.

### The objective it already minimizes

Two of the three structural terms are contact terms, and both are built from the same quantity. For a residue pair $(i,j)$ with distogram logits $z_{ij}$ over bins at midpoints $d_b$, write $p_{ij}$ for the softmax over all bins and $\tilde{p}^{\,c}_{ij}$ for the softmax restricted to bins nearer than a cutoff $c$. The contact score is the cross-entropy between the two:

$$
H^{c}_{ij} \;=\; -\sum_{b} \tilde{p}^{\,c}_{ij}(b)\,\log p_{ij}(b)
$$

This is low when the pair's distance distribution already concentrates below $c$, and high when it does not, so minimizing it pulls a pair into contact. Each term then averages, over a set of rows $R$, the mean of the $k$ smallest such scores available in a set of columns $S$ at sequence separation at least $s$:

$$
\mathcal{C}(R, S, k, c, s) \;=\; \frac{1}{|R|}\sum_{i \in R} \operatorname*{mean}_{k\text{ smallest}} \big\{\, H^{c}_{ij} \;:\; j \in S,\; |i-j| \ge s \,\big\}
$$

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{intra}} = \mathcal{C}(\text{binder},\, \text{binder},\, k{=}2,\, c{=}14\,\text{Å},\, s{=}9),
\qquad
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{inter}} = \mathcal{C}(\text{target},\, \text{binder},\, k{=}1,\, c{=}22\,\text{Å},\, s{=}0)
$$

The two differ in more than their constants. The intra term asks each binder residue for its two best non-local partners inside the binder, which is a request for a folded rather than extended chain. The inter term is averaged over the **target's** residues, each taking its single best partner on the binder, so it asks the binder to cover the target rather than asking the binder to find a foothold.

The third term is a globularity penalty. With $\hat{\mathbb{E}}[d_{ij}^2]$ the distogram's expected squared distance over binder pairs, capped at 27 Å per bin, and $n$ the binder length:

$$
R_g \;=\; \sqrt{\frac{1}{n^{2}}\sum_{i>j} \hat{\mathbb{E}}\big[d_{ij}^{2}\big]},
\qquad
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{glob}} \;=\; \mathrm{ELU}\big(R_g - 2.38\,n^{0.365}\big)
$$

which charges nothing while the binder is more compact than a packed protein of its length and rises once it is not. The three combine at fixed weights:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{struct}} \;=\; 0.5\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{intra}} \;+\; 0.5\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{inter}} \;+\; 0.2\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{glob}}
$$

Read together, they ask for a compact chain that touches itself non-locally and covers the target. None of them mentions secondary structure. There is no term that prefers a helix, and equally no term that prefers anything else — which is what makes the helix excess in @fig-composition a property of something other than an explicit request.

That is also what makes it addressable. The objective is recomputed at every one of the 150 steps from a distogram that already contains the Cα–Cα distances separating a helix from a strand, and the whole path from that distogram back to the sequence is differentiable. So a fourth term can be added to $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{struct}}$ that reads helical geometry off the same tensor and charges for it. Whether that is enough to move designs out of the α-rich basin, and what it costs, is the rest of this section.

### The secondary-structure loss term

In an α helix the Cα atoms of residues $i$ and $i{+}4$ sit about 6.2 Å apart. That is the shortest description of a helix available in a distance map, and it is what the term measures.

Where the cookbook's contact terms score a pair by the cross-entropy $H^{c}_{ij}$, this one uses the plain near-bin mass: $q^{c}_{ij} = \sum_{d_b < c} p_{ij}(b)$, the probability that the pair is closer than $c$. Taking that at $c = 7$ Å along the $i \to i{+}4$ diagonal gives a per-residue helicity. The term is its mean over the binder, added to the structural objective at a fixed weight $w$:

$$
h \;=\; \frac{1}{L-4}\sum_{i=1}^{L-4} q^{\,7\text{Å}}_{i,\,i+4},
\qquad
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{helix}} \;=\; h,
\qquad
\mathcal{L} \;=\; \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{struct}} + w\,h
$$

Three properties of that expression matter later.

**It reads the distogram, not a secondary-structure label.** The composition reported in @fig-composition comes from DSSP, but DSSP cannot be optimized against: it needs backbone coordinates and returns a discrete class, and neither step carries a gradient. So the quantity steered and the quantity measured are deliberately not the same, and the term is only useful to the extent that pushing on one moves the other.

**Every residue counts once.** $h$ is an expected helical-rung fraction, bounded by 0 and 1, and its derivative with respect to any one rung is $1/(L-4)$ whatever the rest of the chain is doing. A residue in a helix at the end of a long binder is charged exactly as much as one in a helix at the start, and no residue is ever charged twice.

**The trailing four residues are excluded rather than counted as zero.** They have no $i{+}4$ partner, so scoring them would report a fixed dilution as though it were an absence of helix.

### Twenty steps of the weight are enough

The onset scan withholds the term and asks whether a fold can still be moved. Withdrawing it asks the opposite: whether a fold the term has produced stays put once the term is gone and the rest of the objective is free to pull the design back. Both ends of this scan are campaigns that exist for other reasons, since a weight withdrawn at step 0 never acts and one never withdrawn is the constant arm at 2.0. The right-hand column of @fig-schedule is that scan.

One step is not enough. Withdrawn at step 1 the design returns to the unsteered arm: final helix 0.798 against 0.824, $p$ = 0.24, and median sheet exactly 0.000. The rebound after withdrawal decays with how long the weight was held, $h$ finishing at 0.730, 0.456, 0.351, 0.219, 0.202 and 0.077 for withdrawals at steps 1, 2, 4, 7, 10 and 20 in @fig-schedule-2.

By step 20 the fold is fixed. Withdrawing there is indistinguishable from never withdrawing, $p$ = 0.198 on final helix, with median sheet 0.547 against 0.591 in @fig-schedule-4 and 26 of 30 designs carrying sheet; the same holds for withdrawals at 40 and 50, $p$ = 0.094 and 0.316. The remaining 130 steps of weight change nothing that thirty seeds can resolve.

Read with the onset scan, commitment is not one moment. The fold is chosen in the first two to four steps and fixed over the following fifteen or so, and a steering term has to be present for both.

### A loss term is a tuning handle, and secondary structure is one thing to tune

The steering result matters less for what it does to helices than for what it says about the method. A differentiable term added to the design loss changed the fold class of the output without retraining anything and without touching the model weights. The handle is the distogram the design loop already optimizes against, and it was sitting there unused.

That reframes the contribution. This is not a paper about helices. It is a worked example of adding a constraint to ESMFold2's binder design algorithm, with the measurements needed to say honestly what the constraint bought and what it cost.

The limits we ran into are part of the example, and they generalize:

- The term stops acting once the property it penalizes is already saturated, so **when** a term applies during the run matters as much as how strongly.
- Pushing harder on one property costs confidence in another, so any added term needs its tradeoff mapped rather than asserted.
- The optimizer will satisfy a loss the cheapest way available, which is not always the way you intended.

Anyone adding a term to this design loop should expect all three.

### A binder is the start of a drug program, not the end

Nothing in this work produces a therapeutic. A design that binds its target with good predicted confidence has cleared the first of many gates. Downstream, a candidate still has to be developable: expressible and soluble at concentration, stable on the shelf, non-aggregating, humanized or otherwise non-immunogenic, free of manufacturing and post-translational liabilities, and specific enough not to bind everything else in the proteome.

Each of those is a property of a sequence or a structure. That is the interesting part, because it is the same kind of object the secondary-structure term acts on. In principle every one of them is expressible as a term on the distogram or on the sequence logits, and added to the same objective in the same place.

Sequence liabilities are the nearest example, and one worth tuning rather than ignoring. Steering the fold also changes the sequences that come out, so a term that optimizes structure alone can quietly degrade a property nobody was watching. We did not write a liability term here, and the designs in this work should not be read as developable. Adding one is the obvious next thing to try, and it would test whether the tuning handle generalizes beyond the property we happened to pick.

That is the claim we want to leave the reader with: ESMFold2's binder design algorithm exposes a place to put constraints, secondary structure is one constraint that demonstrably works there, and the constraints a drug program actually cares about are the reason to care.

### Separating the scorer from the designs

Every confidence number in this notebook comes from ESMFold2 models scoring designs that ESMFold2 produced. A steered design with a low interface pTM has either been made worse by steering or been judged by a model that is less confident about β-rich interfaces, and nothing measured here distinguishes those. A design carries no independent standard of correctness: there is no fact about it that says what its confidence ought to be.

A solved complex does carry one. A heterodimer in the PDB is known to bind, and its deposited coordinates say how close a prediction came. Folding natural binder–target pairs from sequence with the same critic at the same settings the campaigns used, then comparing the confidence it reports against the accuracy it actually achieved — DockQ, or interface RMSD against the deposited complex — turns the question into one about calibration rather than about scores: does the critic's confidence track its own accuracy equally well across fold classes? Confidence that runs low on β-rich complexes the model nonetheless predicts correctly would be scorer bias. Confidence that runs low because the predictions are worse would not. The reference set assembled for Question 1 is the natural starting point, since those chains are already measured by the same code that measures the designs.

Four things make that experiment harder than it looks, and we would want them settled before running it rather than after.

**The scoring set may be in the critic's training data.** ESMFold2 is trained on the PDB, so a natural complex is a held-in example unless it is deliberately excluded. A memorized complex is predicted well and scored confidently, which inflates the apparent calibration and does so for reasons that have nothing to do with fold class.

**Memorization is unlikely to be uniform across fold classes.** What matters is not whether contamination exists but whether it differs between the strata being compared. If α-rich and β-rich binders differ in how long they have been in the PDB, they differ in how likely they are to have been memorized, and a confidence gap will appear or disappear for that reason alone. Any such comparison needs the age distribution of its strata reported alongside the result, and a stated direction for which way the resulting bias runs.

**The cutoff that would define a held-out set is ambiguous.** A temporal holdout needs a date and a meaning for that date, and the two come from different places. The ESMFold2 preprint states its training cutoff in terms of when structures were *released*; the ESM SDK's own mmCIF parser fills a field named `release_date` from `_pdbx_database_status.recvd_initial_deposition_date`, which is when they were *deposited*. Those differ by months to years for structures held before release. Which one governed training is an open question upstream, so a holdout should be cut on deposition date, which is the conservative choice under either reading. Checkpoints also differ in cutoff, and the published checkpoint names do not all state which cutoff they carry.

**β-rich natural binders are scarce, and that is what limits the experiment.** Binders in this size range are mostly mixed α/β; strictly β-rich chains are the smallest of the three classes, and the count is sensitive to where the composition thresholds are drawn. The stratum shrinks further once the comparison is matched on the covariates that drive interface confidence on their own — buried surface area and chain length, both of which differ systematically between α-rich and β-rich natural binders — and shrinks again under any date-based holdout. A design that survives all three cuts is likely to be able to exclude only a large effect, so the informative version of this experiment reports an effect size with an interval rather than a significance test, and says plainly what size of bias it was powered to detect.

A fifth limitation is not about data and cannot be designed away. Natural β-rich binders are closed, interleaved sheets with two strand partners for most strands. The β content this loss term produces is open meander, with fewer partners per strand and no close counterpart in the PDB. Whatever such an experiment finds is therefore a statement about how the critic treats real β folds, which is a well-posed question, and not a verdict on these designs. A well-scored natural β complex would not make the steered designs' low confidence wrong, and a badly-scored one would not make the designs good.

## An open question: objective or weights?

Everything here changes behavior without changing the model. The steering happens in the design loop, on top of frozen weights, and that is worth naming as a choice rather than a default, because there is an obvious alternative: retrain or fine-tune so that the model produces the distribution you want natively.

The two routes are not equivalent, and our results show some of the difference. Steering from the objective fights the model's prior instead of altering it, which may be why interface confidence pays a price, and why the optimizer sometimes satisfies the term in ways we did not intend. A model whose weights had learned the target distribution would presumably not need to be argued with in the same way.

But the comparison is lopsided on cost. Adding a term to the loss is a few lines and a single campaign. Retraining a structure prediction model of this scale means substantial compute, a training corpus assembled for the property you want, and revalidation of everything the base model was already good at, with the risk of degrading it. For a property you might only want occasionally, or want in three mutually exclusive variants, that is a steep price. Post-hoc terms are also composable, inspectable, and trivially reversible, which weight updates are not.

So we would pose it as a question rather than answer it. Which behaviors belong in the weights, and which belong in the objective? Is there a principled boundary, drawn perhaps by how fundamental a property is or how often it is wanted, or is the line mostly economic and therefore likely to move as training costs fall? We do not know, and the honest position from this work is that the objective route is cheap enough to be worth exhausting before anyone reaches for the weights.
